Stolid

/STOL-id/ - the stress falls on STOL · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Stolid means expressing little sensibility, unemotional.

Through wins, losses, and a bench-clearing brawl, the pitching coach stayed stolid, arms crossed in the same corner of the dugout.

Worked Example

The bomb-squad veteran narrated the whole disposal in the tone of a man reading a parts list—wire, clip, breathe—and his stolid delivery steadied every rookie on the line.

Stolid is not calm exactly—it's the absence of visible feeling. Where a serene face radiates peace, a stolid one simply gives nothing out: no flinch, no grin, no tell. The word often praises steadiness, but it can shade toward 'dull' if warmth never appears.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

unemotional: the plain umbrella word for feeling kept off the face

expressionless: nothing readable on the face at this moment

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

demonstrative: shows feelings openly and physically

emotional: feelings near the surface, quick to spill

Where it sits · how much feeling still shows through — matter-of-fact → stolid → expressionless

matter-of-fact vs. stolid: Matter-of-fact is milder than stolid: a matter-of-fact nurse delivers the news plainly but can still smile on the way out, while a stolid one shows almost no feeling at all.

expressionless vs. stolid: Expressionless goes further than matter-of-fact—an expressionless face is a blank wall showing nothing at all, while a stolid one still leaks the occasional shrug.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — stolid

Root — stolid: dull, immovable (Latin stolidus)

Put it together

Put it together: Stolid arrived whole from Latin stolidus, 'immovable, dull as a block'—there is nothing to peel off. Romans used it as an insult for the slow-witted; English kept the immovability and softened the insult, leaving a word for faces that give nothing away.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Latin stolidus left no everyday English descendants—its distant cousin stultus ('foolish') survives only in the rare verb stultify—so stolid stands alone on the family tree.

Strength Check

Word Choice

neutral, can shade critical

Use stolid for people who show almost nothing—praise when it means unshakable, a nudge when it means unreachable. Keep the unit's calm family straight: placid people feel at ease and look it; serene people glow with peace; stolid people may feel plenty, but the face declines to report it. Taciturn is the same economy applied to words instead of expressions.
